learning_objective: 🎯 Learn how organizations ensure their actual performance matches their planned targets, and how they fix things when they go off track!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Comparing actual performance with planned standards, finding out the deviations (differences), and taking corrective action to ensure goals are met.
They are inseparable twins. Planning without controlling is meaningless (no one checks the work). Controlling without planning is blind (no targets to compare against).
1. Setting Performance Standards (targets) -> 2. Measurement of Actual Performance -> 3. Comparing Actual Performance with Standards.

Critical Point Control (focusing on Key Result Areas - KRAs that impact the whole business) and Management by Exception (if you try to control everything, you control nothing; only major deviations should go to top management).
If the deviation is unacceptable, find the cause (e.g., defective machinery, lack of training) and fix it. If the original standard was unrealistic, revise the standard.

fun_activity.title: 🎯 The Bow and Arrow Target
fun_activity.instructions: Your goal (Standard) is 90% in exams. You scored 80% (Actual). The gap is 10% (Deviation). List 2 reasons for this deviation (Causes) and 2 actions you will take next time (Corrective Action)!

exam_tips: 📌 'Management by Exception' (MBE) means managers should only step in when deviations are significant. Minor issues should be handled by lower levels.
📌 'Critical Point Control' (CPC) focuses on areas that are critical to success. A 5% increase in production cost is more critical than a 15% increase in postal charges.
📌 Remember: Controlling is both backward-looking (checking past actions) and forward-looking (improving future planning).
quick_recap: ⭐ Controlling does not mean restricting employees; it means keeping the organization on the right track.
⭐ Standards can be quantitative (units produced, cost) or qualitative (customer satisfaction, employee morale).
⭐ Measurement of performance should be done in the same units in which standards were set.
